before: Prioritise the evidence needed to decide whether restrictions are justified: attributable risk, existing-control limitations, incremental benefit, applicant and regulator cost, and workforce response. The 6 October email records a request for stronger evidence to warrant regulating carpentry; this is a reason to test the case, not proof that regulation is either necessary or ineffective. [7]
after: The departmental reply refers the evidence question to Chapter 2 of the historical RIS. That chapter identifies material concerns, while acknowledging data and attribution limits, including risk-selected inspections and dispute-counting effects. This supports examining the problem; it does not itself measure the incremental defect reduction from registration. Retain the request for current evidence and an evaluation against alternatives. The 6 October email records calls for stronger evidence and contrary views. [2, pp. 34–46; 7; 9]

before: DTP estimates more than 20,000 carpenters in Victoria. This is a departmental estimate in the presentation, not a verified count of residential renovation practitioners. after: DTP’s slides estimate more than 20,000 carpenters in Victoria. Courtney Gleeson’s reply refers the evidence question to the historical RIS. Reconcile dates, occupational coverage, roles and registration categories before forecasting BPC, assessor or training demand. [2, p. 30; 6, slide 6; 9]

before: Set transition duration using cohort size, verified gaps, safety risk and regulator and training capacity. after: Set transition duration using cohort size, verified gaps, safety risk and regulator and training capacity. A five-year pathway was raised by a meeting participant and also appears in the historical RIS, with a time-limited application period and training-plan conditions. Neither source establishes a current adopted duration. Staging should not permit unproven safety-critical competence or become indefinite provisional status. [2, pp. 71–72; 5, DTPM-022 and 033; 7; 9]

before: For future entrants, a completed carpentry apprenticeship with Certificate III is the initiative’s preferred foundation. That preference should be distinguished from transition for existing workers whose learning may include qualifications, supervised experience and on-the-job learning. Any equivalence route must reliably demonstrate the required competence; tenure or a certificate alone is not sufficient. The final treatment of future non-apprenticeship routes remains for policy review. [6, slide 6]
after: For future entrants, this initiative recommends a completed carpentry apprenticeship with Certificate III as the entry requirement. For the existing workforce, provide a separate route through reliably verified equivalent competence and targeted training or experience for identified gaps. Tenure alone is not sufficient, and competent existing workers should not repeat a full qualification unnecessarily. This is our proposed entry rule, not a government decision. The historical RIS describes assessment and training plans for transition, but its settings require current confirmation. [2, pp. 71–72; 6, slide 6; 9]

before: Slide 3 distinguishes the existing registered-builder tier from proposed subcontractor registration and employee licensing. It shows consumer contracting for carpentry over $10,000 only for the builder tier, subcontracting with a builder for builders and proposed subcontractors, and performance of carpentry work for all three tiers. Apprentices are noted as outside the proposed registration and licensing requirements. This is the presentation’s permission summary, not a complete statement of current law. The partial meeting transcript’s separate under-$10,000 statement remains unresolved against the deck; permits, insurance, corporate roles and commencement need authoritative confirmation. [5, DTPM-015–019; 6, slide 3]
after: Slide 3 summarises proposed builder, subcontractor and employee permissions, but does not show a below-threshold contracting column. Courtney Gleeson directs us to historical RIS sections 1.3 and 1.3.2 and Table 0.1. The table shows subcontractors contracting for carpentry under $10,000 under the then-existing scheme, with new registration and disciplinary obligations proposed separately. This helps explain the meeting statement rather than establishing a contradiction with the slides. Current law and proposed changes must be checked separately; permits, insurance, corporate roles and carpentry commencement remain distinct questions. [2, pp. 28–31; 5, DTPM-015–019; 6, slide 3; 9]

before: Match each requirement to the risk it controls and the burden it imposes. Low-value work can still create serious technical risk; commercial exposure and technical scope require separate analysis. The slides’ over-$10,000 contracting column does not define safe work or resolve all below-threshold arrangements. Seek authoritative clarification before treating it as a complete legal rule. [6, slides 3 and 5]
after: Match each requirement to the risk it controls and the burden it imposes. Current regulation 6 fixes the major domestic building contract threshold at $10,000; section 3 defines a major contract by an amount above that threshold, and section 29 requires registration authorising the work. Separate draft contract regulations propose $20,000. The departmental reply reports expected commencement on 31 March 2027; that is not a carpenter-scheme commencement date or proof that the threshold has changed. Low-value work can still create serious technical risk. [9–12]

before: • Use proportionate verification of qualifications, apprenticeship outcomes and relevant experience. Add technical testing or other reliable evidence only where the authorised scope and applicant risk warrant it. Do not require every worker to complete a universal battery of assessments.
